source_title: Sample Interview: Building PaySwift Across Three Markets
text:
Host: Amara, thanks for joining us. Let's start at the beginning. Where did PaySwift come from?

Amara Okonkwo: It came from a very ordinary frustration. In 2016 I was working as a treasury analyst at a bank in Lagos, and I watched merchants queue for forty minutes to deposit cash takings. These were people running pharmacies and hardware shops. The float sitting in their tills was capital they could not use. I kept asking why a shop owner in Surulere could not settle to a bank account the same evening, and nobody could give me a good answer beyond the fact that the rails had never been built.

Host: So you left the bank.

Amara Okonkwo: I left in January 2017, with two colleagues. Chidi handled engineering, Ngozi handled compliance, and I did everything else. We incorporated PaySwift in March 2017 in Lagos. Our first product was not the payments product at all. It was a reconciliation tool. We would take a merchant's paper ledger, digitise it overnight, and hand it back reconciled in the morning. It was almost entirely manual. But it taught us where the money actually leaked, which was not fraud, it was mismatched settlement timing.

Host: How did you get from there to processing payments?

Amara Okonkwo: We needed a licence, and that took most of 2018. The Central Bank of Nigeria granted us a switching and processing licence in November 2018. That was the unlock. From that point we could settle merchant transactions directly rather than riding on somebody else's rails and paying for the privilege. We launched the merchant product in February 2019 with about four hundred shops in Lagos.

Host: And the expansion beyond Nigeria?

Amara Okonkwo: Ghana in 2021, Kenya in 2022. I would say Ghana was harder than we expected and Kenya was easier. Ghana was harder because we assumed the Nigerian playbook would transfer, and it did not. Merchant density is lower, the mobile money habit was already deeply established, and we were arriving as an outsider offering something they thought they already had. We had to rebuild the product around mobile money interoperability rather than card acceptance. Kenya was easier precisely because we had learned that lesson and did not repeat it.

Host: What did that cost you?

Amara Okonkwo: About eighteen months and, I would guess, four million dollars we did not need to spend. But I do not entirely regret it. The Ghana failure is why the platform is now built as market-specific modules on a shared core, and that architecture is the only reason we could enter Kenya in seven months.

Host: You raised a Series B in 2023.

Amara Okonkwo: We closed a forty-two million dollar Series B in September 2023, led by a growth fund out of London with participation from two pan-African funds. We had crossed a hundred and ten thousand active merchants by then, and monthly processed volume was around eight hundred million dollars annualised.

Host: What is the thing people get wrong about building here?

Amara Okonkwo: They assume the constraint is technology. It is not. The constraint is trust and distribution. Our single most effective growth channel was never digital marketing. It was hiring former market traders as field agents, because a shop owner will believe someone who has stood behind the same kind of counter. We have four hundred and sixty field agents now. That is not a technology decision, it is an anthropology decision, and the companies that miss it stay small.

Host: Last question. What would you tell yourself in 2017?

Amara Okonkwo: Get the licence first. We spent a year building a product we could not legally run at scale. The regulator is not your obstacle, the regulator is your moat, and I did not understand that until much later.
